titre: The File She Refused to Sign
accroche: In 1960, an FDA pharmacologist refuses to approve a sedative already sold in 46 countries, without yet knowing why she is right
contenu_vulgarise:
On August 1, 1960, Frances Kelsey joins the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, among the handful of physicians responsible for reviewing applications for marketing authorization of new drugs. A month later, on September 8, 1960, she is assigned one of her very first applications: Kevadon, the American trade name of thalidomide, a sedative already sold in forty-six countries, recommended for insomnia, morning sickness, and just about everything else, from asthma to alcoholism.

## A File That Does Not Convince

The law requires the manufacturer to prove the drug's safety before it goes on the market; Kelsey judges that the data supplied by the company Richardson-Merrell are insufficient, notably on the effects of prolonged use and use during pregnancy. She refuses to approve the file and demands additional evidence. The company, which was hoping for a quick commercial launch, puts repeated pressure on her and her superiors. Kelsey maintains her refusal, month after month, with no argument other than a methodical doubt about the quality of the evidence provided. The molecule, meanwhile, continues to be distributed to about 20,000 American patients in unregulated clinical trials run by volunteer physicians.

In November 1961, the German pediatrician Widukind Lenz establishes a link between thalidomide taken during pregnancy and a rare and spectacular malformation: children are born with limbs reduced to mere stumps attached directly to the trunk (phocomelia). The Australian obstetrician William McBride independently reaches the same conclusion the same year. Within a few years, more than 10,000 children worldwide are born with malformations attributed to thalidomide.

## A File Left Closed

Because Kelsey never signed the authorization, thalidomide is never marketed on a large scale in the United States: the unregulated trials produce a handful of cases of malformations there, out of all proportion to the disaster observed in the forty-six countries where the drug was freely on sale.

## The Shift

The episode leads not only to the recognition of Kelsey, decorated by President Kennedy in 1962: it durably changes the law. That same year, the U.S. Congress passes the Kefauver-Harris Amendments, which require manufacturers for the first time to prove not only the safety but also the efficacy of a drug before it goes on the market, on the basis of controlled clinical trials. The principle that seems elementary today, that a drug must prove its benefit, not merely the absence of proof of its danger, flows directly from an administrative refusal held for more than a year, before anyone knew that refusal to be justified.

repere.texte: Marketed in forty-six countries in the late 1950s, thalidomide is behind more than 10,000 congenital malformations worldwide before its withdrawal, a disaster the United States escaped on a large scale thanks to a single administrative refusal.
repere.source: Embryo Project Encyclopedia, Arizona State University — “US Regulatory Response to Thalidomide (1950-2000)”

carte.punch: A refusal to sign, held for over a year, spared the United States a pharmaceutical disaster.
carte.idee: In 1960, Frances Kelsey refuses to authorize the sale of thalidomide in the United States, judging the file insufficient. A year later, it is discovered that this sedative, sold in 46 countries, caused severe malformations in more than 10,000 children. Her refusal leads to the American law still in force.

quiz.question: Why did Kelsey's refusal concretely spare the United States, even though thalidomide was already circulating there by other means?
choix: Because she had all distribution of thalidomide banned, including on an experimental basis
Because her refusal prevented the drug's open sale in pharmacies, limiting exposure to unregulated trials
Because she personally warned every American physician of the dangers of thalidomide
Because the United States had already banned the import of all German drugs since 1945
quiz.explication: Kelsey did not stop the unregulated clinical trials already under way; about 20,000 American patients had received the molecule that way. Her refusal prevented open sale in pharmacies, which limited exposure to a fraction of what it would have been with commercial distribution across the country, as in the 46 countries where the drug was freely on sale.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What event leads, in November 1961, to establishing a link between thalidomide and congenital malformations?
choix: The publication of a study commissioned by the FDA itself
A U.S. Congress inquiry into clinical trials
The independent work of the German pediatrician Widukind Lenz
An internal report from the company Richardson-Merrell
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text indicates that in November 1961 it is the German pediatrician Widukind Lenz who establishes this link, followed the same year by the Australian obstetrician William McBride, who independently reached the same conclusion.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What concretely does the American law passed in 1962 change, following the thalidomide episode?
choix: It requires proof of a drug's efficacy, in addition to its safety
It bans the sale of any drug tested outside the United States
It makes the randomized clinical trial mandatory for every sedative
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Kefauver-Harris Amendments of 1962 require for the first time proof not only of safety but also of the efficacy of a drug before it goes on the market, on the basis of controlled clinical trials.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How did the company Richardson-Merrell react to Kelsey's refusal to approve the file?
choix: It permanently withdrew its application for authorization
It put repeated pressure on her and her superiors
It went to court to contest the decision
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that the company, which was hoping for a quick commercial launch, put repeated pressure on Kelsey and her superiors, without getting her to reverse her refusal.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many children were born worldwide with malformations attributed to thalidomide, according to the entry?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text indicates that within a few years, more than 10,000 children worldwide were born with malformations attributed to thalidomide, notably in the 46 countries where it was freely sold.
